OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant, 'PA') and her minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellants 'AAs'), all citizens of Nigeria, appeal the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated June 30, 2020.

[2] The PA is the Designated Representative (DR) of her minor children, the AAs. The AAs rely on the evidence of the PA for their appeals.

[3] The PA fears returning to Nigeria as she fears that the family of her deceased husband will harm her and her children. Prior to their departure from Nigeria, and the death of the PA's husband in Canada, her husband's family wanted to perform traditional rituals on her husband and their children. On XXXX XXXX, 2016 the PA's husband was notified that the oracle had chosen him to replace the late Chef priest and that his daughter must be circumcised, and his sons drink a concoction. The Appellants fled from Nigeria, via the United States of America (USA) to Canada and filed for protection on April 12, 2018. The PA's husband passed away in Canada and now his family also blame her for the death.

[4] The RPD determined that the Appellants had an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Port Harcourt and dismissed the claims.

[45] Objectively, Nigeria is the most populated country in Africa, with expected growth from 186 million inhabitants in 2016 to 392 million in 2050,38 concentrated in the south and southwest of the country.39 The Igbo and Yoruba tribes are the second and third largest tribes in Nigeria, together numbering well over half the population. This makes anonymity from family members easier even if some family live in one of the more populous cities. Importantly, Nigeria has a poor infrastructure which results in difficulty in locating persons city to city;40and a very inefficient property registration system.41

[46] While the reference by the PA to technology as a means to locate her was general, the Appellants can take any steps they feel necessary to mitigate their exposure, for example, on social media, which could establish a location. It has been held by the Federal Court that maintaining privacy on social media is reasonable and not a violation of any right or freedom or akin to living like a fugitive.42 The PA's family is supportive of her, and they do not need to disclose her location either.

[47] While the PA indicated that there is a risk of criminality in Port Harcourt, IFA must be examined in the context of personal risk to the Appellants. No personal risk was established under ss. 97(1) of the IRPA.

[48] As such, they face a generalized risk of being victims of terrorism or criminality in Port Harcourt, the same risk that is posed to them in Nigeria in general. Generalized crime does not rise to the very high level of unreasonableness as contemplated by the Federal Court of Appeal, which sets a very high threshold for the unreasonableness test: "It requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area. In addition, it requires actual and concrete evidence of such conditions."43

[49] Overall, I find insufficient evidence has been provided by the Appellants in establishing that they face a serious possibility of persecution in Port Harcourt; or on a balance of probabilities, face a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment of punishment or risk of torture in Port Harcourt.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant, 'PA') and her minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellants 'AAs'), all citizens of Nigeria, appeal the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated June 30, 2020.
[2] The PA is the Designated Representative (DR) of her minor children, the AAs. The AAs rely on the evidence of the PA for their appeals.

[3] The PA fears returning to Nigeria as she fears that the family of her deceased husband will harm her and her children. Prior to their departure from Nigeria, and the death of the PA's husband in Canada, her husband's family wanted to perform traditional rituals on her husband and their children. On XXXX XXXX, 2016 the PA's husband was notified that the oracle had chosen him to replace the late Chef priest and that his daughter must be circumcised, and his sons drink a concoction. The Appellants fled from Nigeria, via the United States of America (USA) to Canada and filed for protection on April 12, 2018. The PA's husband passed away in Canada and now his family also blame her for the death.
[4] The RPD determined that the Appellants had an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Port Harcourt and dismissed the claims.

[5] The Appellants ask that I allow the appeal and find them to be Convention refugee or persons in need of protection; or in the alternative, that I allow the appeal and remit the matter back to the RPD for re-determination.1

[6] After an independent review of the record on the standard of correctness,2 I find that Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection as they have an IFA in Port Harcourt.
NEW EVIDENCE
The evidence presented by the Appellants is rejected.
[7] The Appellants seek to admit the letters of Dr. XXXX XXXX XXXX and Dr. XXXX XXXX3, both are dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020.

[8] According to the law,4 I can only accept evidence that:
i. arose after the RPD decision; or
ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or
iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.5
[9] Both medical letters provided are dated after the RPD decision of June 30, 2020 and are therefore new on their face. They speak to the treatment of the PA for diabetes.

[10] While Dr. XXXX indicates that the PA is a patient of the clinic, the writer does not indicate when the treatment began. From the inter-related medical letter from Dr. XXXX XXXX, however, it can be extrapolated that the condition and treatment is not new, as it is confirmed by Dr. XXXX that the PA has been treated since 2018 for XXXX. That would be two years prior to the RPD decision being rendered and long before the RPD hearing.

[11] The onus is on the Appellants to establish how their evidence is new and meets the requirements. While the Appellants have provided submissions as to how the diabetes diagnosis of the PA may impact the reasonableness of an IFA in Nigeria,6 the Memorandum is silent on establishing why the medical information could not have reasonably been provided to the RPD.

[12] In considering whether the evidence arose after the rejection of the claim, I do not restrict my analysis to the date on the proposed new evidence. In my view, a document's "newness" cannot be tested solely by the date of its creation; what is important is the event or circumstance sought to be proved by the evidence.7 Old evidence remains old evidence, even if it is placed in a new document with a recent date.

[13] I note that the Appellants were represented by counsel at their hearing, and it is not clear from the Appellants' submission why evidence they view as important for establishing a successful claim, would not have been presented.

[14] I have also reviewed the RPD hearing audio record and note that it contains no evidence of the PA advising or attempting to advise the RPD that she had any pending medical appointments or any medical condition that was under treatment. Further, the Appellants made no request for additional time to seek or submit any medical reports to the RPD.

[15] As a result, I find that the Appellants have failed to meet their burden of proof to explain why these reports are "new" and were not reasonably available prior to the rejection of the claim. The proposed evidence thus does not meet the statutory requirements and is therefore not admitted as new evidence. I have no discretion to admit evidence that does not meet the requirements.
ORAL HEARING

[16] As the new evidence is not admissible in accordance with subsection 110(4) of Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), I have no jurisdiction, under ss.110 (6), to hold a hearing.
ISSUES IN APPEAL
ANALYSIS

[18] The Appellants argue that the RPD erred by failing to consider subjective fear and credibility. This is not an accurate characterization of the RPD decision or of the examination conducted by the RPD contained in the RPD hearing audio record.

[19] Subjective fear and the failure of the Appellants to claim in the USA was considered by the RPD and addressed in the RPD Decision.8 In fact, while the PA could not offer clear explanation in her oral testimony as to why she and her husband spent nine months in the USA without filing a claim for protection9, and three months at risk of deportation, the RPD panel chose not to draw an adverse finding in her decision.

[20] I further note that the Federal Court of Appeal held in Kanagaratnum that it is acceptable for an IFA analysis to be conducted without first determining the credibility of a claimant's allegations of persecution.10

[21] While credibility is not considered in totality, in my review, I have considered the evidence relating to the agents of persecution in conjunction with the IFA of Port Harcourt, and whether sufficient credible evidence has been provided to establish the profile of the agents of persecution and to rebut the safety and reasonableness of Port Harcourt as an IFA.
Internal Flight Alternative (IFA)
Legal Test
[22] In assessing an IFA, I have applied the two-pronged test cited in Rasaratnam11 suitably modified to take account of section 97 of the IRPA.

[23] I must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no serious possibility of the Appellant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the Appellant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture, believed on substantial grounds to exist, in the IFA.

[24] Moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all of the circumstances, including those particular to the Appellant, for her to seek refuge there. Both prongs must be satisfied to find that the Appellants have an IFA.

[25] I am also mindful that the burden of proof rests with the Appellants to show that they do not have an IFA. The finding of an IFA must be based on a distinct evaluation of a region for that purpose, remaining mindful of the Appellants' identities. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option. The Appellants are not required to encounter great physical danger or to undergo undue hardship in traveling there or staying there.12

[26] I note that a new version of the National Documentation Package (NDP)13 was released after the Appellants perfected their appeal. Pursuant to Zhang14, I have considered whether there is any recent information reflecting a change in country conditions, such that would require me to give notice to the Appellants, and I do not see that submissions are warranted.
No serious possibility of persecution, or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or of torture in Port Harcourt:
Agents of persecution

[27] The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in its conclusion on the reach and power of the agents of persecution. They submit that as her deceased husband's family members located them in Lagos, and harmed the PA's father, that shows their strength.

[28] The Appellants submit that the RPD failed to consider the Affidavit of the PA's husband and his Basis of Claim (BoC) form that was prepared prior to his death. It is argued that these are sufficient to establish the profile of the agents of persecution.15 Furthermore, the Appellants allege that the RPD ignored the evidence provided by the PA's mother in her Affidavit16 which contained the threatening note directed at the PA's while in Canada.
[29] While the RPD refers to a consideration of all the supporting evidence, I note that there is no specific analysis of the documentation contained in the decision, as stated by the Appellants.

[30] As a result, I have reviewed the supporting documents that have been provided by the Appellants and conclude that they, in conjunction with the PA's oral testimony, provide sufficient credible evidence on events involving the agents of persecution; nor of their interest and reach all over Nigeria, as alleged.

[31] On its face, I find that the Affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX17 is not reliable or probative. The Affidavit heading is written over the stamp of the Solicitors and Notary, which removes the seal/stamp as a security featured. It should be stamped on top. In addition, the photograph of the Affiant's should be under the seal and not on top of it.18

[32] There is no space contained between 'XXXX and 'XXXX in the heading, and the last line refers to the Oath and Affirmation Act, however, the objective evidence indicates that the proper name is 'Oaths' Law, Oath is plural.19

[33] The Affidavit of XXXX XXXX,20 refers to the Oaths Law of Lagos State 2003; and the Affidavit of Mrs. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX references Oath Law of 2015.21 None of the Affidavits reference the correct phrase and year.

[34] The objective evidence confirms that Affidavits in Nigeria must contain the affiant's name, trade, profession, residence, and nationality.22 The Affidavits provided by the Appellants do not include reference to trade or profession. Fraudulently obtained Affidavits are widely available in Nigeria, and even court officials are motivated in producing false Affidavits for personal gain.23 As a result, I do not find these Affidavits on their face sufficient credible evidence of the nature, within reach and power of the agents of persecution.

[35] I also note that the PA's husband writes in his Affidavit that he went immediately to the Alagolo police station in Ipaja, before being transferred to Ikeja for further investigation, where he made his Affidavit.

[36] The police report provided24 is from the Ikeja police department and the extract entry indicates that it was all filed at XXXX XXXX XXXX pm on the day of the attack. This contrasts with the PA's oral testimony on the sequence of events, which does not support their attendances at two police stations and the completion of an Affidavit all by XXXX XXXX XXXX pm,25 the recorded time entry on the document.

[37] In oral testimony that PA indicated that on XXXX XXXX, 2016, her husband had taken all of the family out to a restaurant (her husband's BoC narrative says shopping),26 and on return, her father was found beaten and unconscious.27 Both the PA and the BoC narrative indicate that her father had to be taken to the hospital;28 however, there is no report in evidence for this admission.

[38] The PA testified that the police investigated the assault on her father; the inspector came to the house, and she believed that there was an arrest.29 She was vague and offered no details despite residing in Nigeria for XXXX months after this event.

[39] The PA could not explain her evidence of an arrest in contrast to the BoC narrative which specifically indicates no investigation or arrest.30 I find that the RPD had good reason to find insufficient credible evidence presented on the agents of persecution and their interest and reach, as both the supporting evidence and oral evidence was deficient.

[40] I note also that the Appellants continued to reside at the same address after the XXXX 2016 assault on the PA's father, for XXXX more months until their departure to the USA.31 There was ample opportunity for the agents of persecution to locate them prior to their departure from Nigeria also, shows that they so desired.

[41] The threatening note from XXXX XXXX,32 provided to the PA by her mother,33 was delivered to the PA's known family location. The note specifically mentions 'wherever she may be'; indicating that the writer does not know the location of the PA and her children. While there are anomalies with all the supporting Affidavits provided, even if this note is taken at face, it supports that the PA's location is not known, and the oracle has not successfully assisted the agents of persecution in locating them.

[42] I also note that there is no objective evidence supporting the powers of idol worshippers to use oracles to locate individuals and harm them. If this were true, it would be reasonably expected to be widely reported in the objective materials.

[43] The conclusion reached by the RPD is further supported by the PA's oral evidence at the hearing. While the PA had been married for fourteen years, she was vague in her description of the agents of persecution, vague about what they want to do, and the powers they wield. She could not articulate with any detail what the traditional rights are;34 the PA was vague on whom else had undergone these rituals in the family;35 and offered little spontaneous and detailed evidence as to how anyone would locate her in Port Harcourt. She referred to technology and the oracle as the main means, but was unable to elaborate.36 There was an allegation of a connection to the government, however no details were provided, and she stated that only her deceased husband knows the details.37

[44] The Appellants have been outside Nigeria for almost four years and allege one attempt by the agents of persecution to reach out to them, two years ago. Therefore, there is insufficient credible evidence of an ongoing search for them in Nigeria, and overall there is insufficient evidence that the agents of persecution have the interest, or means to locate the Appellant in Port Harcourt, thousands of kilometers away from Lagos.

[45] Objectively, Nigeria is the most populated country in Africa, with expected growth from 186 million inhabitants in 2016 to 392 million in 2050,38 concentrated in the south and southwest of the country.39 The Igbo and Yoruba tribes are the second and third largest tribes in Nigeria, together numbering well over half the population. This makes anonymity from family members easier even if some family live in one of the more populous cities. Importantly, Nigeria has a poor infrastructure which results in difficulty in locating persons city to city;40and a very inefficient property registration system.41

[46] While the reference by the PA to technology as a means to locate her was general, the Appellants can take any steps they feel necessary to mitigate their exposure, for example, on social media, which could establish a location. It has been held by the Federal Court that maintaining privacy on social media is reasonable and not a violation of any right or freedom or akin to living like a fugitive.42 The PA's family is supportive of her, and they do not need to disclose her location either.

[47] While the PA indicated that there is a risk of criminality in Port Harcourt, IFA must be examined in the context of personal risk to the Appellants. No personal risk was established under ss. 97(1) of the IRPA.

[48] As such, they face a generalized risk of being victims of terrorism or criminality in Port Harcourt, the same risk that is posed to them in Nigeria in general. Generalized crime does not rise to the very high level of unreasonableness as contemplated by the Federal Court of Appeal, which sets a very high threshold for the unreasonableness test: "It requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area. In addition, it requires actual and concrete evidence of such conditions."43

[49] Overall, I find insufficient evidence has been provided by the Appellants in establishing that they face a serious possibility of persecution in Port Harcourt; or on a balance of probabilities, face a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment of punishment or risk of torture in Port Harcourt.
Port Harcourt is reasonable in all of the circumstances

[50] The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in consideration of all the evidence in determining Port Harcourt a reasonable IFA for these Appellants. They submit that high unemployment, difficulties for the PA in having three young children; and being non-indigenes44 will be obstacles to securing employment and social services for the Appellants.

[51] I note that the threshold to establish that Port Harcourt is unreasonable, is a high one for the Appellants.45 It is not enough that they cannot find suitable work there or have no friends there.46

[52] The PA is from a Christian family and is Yoruba, and Yoruba is the largest ethnic group in the south-west of Nigeria. Nigeria is extremely diverse with hundreds of ethnic groups however.47 She is university educated and has a total of 16 years of education,48 well above the national average. The PA worked as a teacher for 7 years in the Lagos public school system, prior to coming to Canada.49

[53] With her skills she is not dependent on government employment and she identified that she preferred to send her children to private schools which are common in Nigeria also.50 I do not agree with the Appellants' submission that the PA is limited to trading or driving a taxi with her skills.

[54] While indigeneship influences access to employment in the civil and public service areas,51 this does not impact the PA who can work in the private sector teaching, or who has a broad educational background that can lead to other private sector employment.

[55] Indeed, the objective evidence confirms that finding gainful employment in Nigeria's large cities "is facilitated by a good level of 'education, experience, or expertise."52 Speaking and knowledge of English is an asset.53 The PA falls squarely into this group.54

[56] While it is acknowledged that single female heads of household's face difficulties that are unique from intact families; and may face discrimination in obtaining housing55, there is no limitation or constraints on accessing public services.56 Professional and well educated women do not experience as many problems as heads of households, especially in the south where the population is richer and better educated.57 Statistically in Nigeria, women who are divorced, separated or widowed have an 81% chance of being employed, and this increases with post-secondary education, as the PA is.58

[57] Furthermore, the Appellants resided for nine months in the USA, the PA's husband worked illegally, reflecting a certain resourcefulness, while the PA volunteered at her church. She stated that they were able to obtain church community assistance in the USA which facilitated their life there.59 As noted by the RPD, and not challenged by the Appellants, Port Harcourt offers an active and vibrant Christian community.

[58] The Appellants argue that the objective evidence confirms there is discrimination towards non-indigene residents in Nigeria, and I agree that the evidence is mixed in this regard. There is some evidence that the importance of indigeneship is elevated in some areas of life; however, it is also noted objectively, that internal migration in Nigeria is the norm, and in most urban Nigerian cities issues of indigeneity are less evidence, except at the local government level.60

[59] Furthermore, "[n]on-indigenes are entitled to access essential public services, including health care, primary and secondary education," and "non-indigeneity does not influence access to health services," which "is largely a function of the ability to pay, even in public hospitals."61

[60] I find insufficient credible evidence establishing that the cost of housing and a lack of access to services renders Port Harcourt an unreasonable IFA either, bearing in mind that the Federal Court has held that a lack of financial resources does not render an IFA unreasonable.62

[61] While the PA is a single mother, given her closest family ties remain her mother and brother in Nigeria, and she has been functioning as an independent single adult household for almost three years since her husband's death, I do not find that her change in marital status renders Port Harcourt unreasonable given her particular circumstances.

[62] For all of the reasons outlined above, I am satisfied that the second part of the Rasaratnam63 test has been met and that it would not be objectively unreasonable in all of the circumstances for the Appellants, to relocate to Port Harcourt.
CONCLUSION

[63] I dismiss the appeals and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
